https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=497.draft: The premortem framing maps onto this well. Instead of asking what you'd do if Claude Code disappeared, assume it already has and write down the reasons. Klein, Sonkin and Johnson argue it's easier to explain why something happened than to generate scenarios for what might happen, which is exactly the asymmetry that makes "what's my fallback" so hard to answer honestly. Two conditions from their paper matter here. Problem reframing: the exercise only works if you commit to the failure being real, not hypothetical. And a cognitively diverse group: if you run this alone you'll surface the problems you already suspect. The people who'd notice your blind spots are the ones who see your work but don't share your enthusiasm for the tool. A secondary benefit they note is reduced overconfidence, which is the actual risk in a dependency that feels like a body part. The failure modes worth listing aren't just "the service goes down" but the skills and context that quietly stop being maintained while the tool works.

One thing worth being careful about with Monte Carlo plan comparisons: the ensemble average across many simulated paths is not the same as the time average for any single path. Wealth processes are non-ergodic, so a plan can look fine on expected value while most individual paths end badly, or vice versa. That matters for how you present results. If the simulator reports a median or a success rate, that is closer to a time-average question (what happens to me over my life) than a mean terminal balance is. A mean terminal balance is an ensemble statistic and can be dominated by a small number of very good paths. For the mortgage prepayment versus taxable investing comparison specifically, the ranking of the two strategies can flip depending on whether you look at the mean across scenarios or the typical outcome for one person. Showing a distribution of paths, or at least percentiles, rather than a single expected number would make the tool's answers much more honest about risk.
